title: A Diarrhea Workup Found a Windsock-Shaped Pouch Hanging Inside a 76-Year-Old's Small Intestine
text:
A Diarrhea Workup Found a Windsock-Shaped Pouch Hanging Inside a 76-Year-Old's Small Intestine
A 76-year-old woman with a year of chronic diarrhea underwent a routine upper endoscopy, and the camera found something that looked like it belonged at an airfield. A thin pouch of tissue hung inside her duodenum, the first stretch of the small intestine, shaped like the wind socks pilots use to read the wind.
Doctors at Mayo Clinic in Scottsdale, Arizona, identified it as an intraluminal duodenal diverticulum, an exceedingly rare anomaly thought to form before birth. Their report, published February 13, 2026, in Cureus by Pierce L. Claassen, Francisco C. Ramirez, and Terry L. Jue, describes a structure she had likely carried, unknowingly, for her entire life.
A Year of Loose Stools and No Clear Answer
She was referred to a gastroenterology clinic after about a year of intermittent diarrhea, passing three to five loose stools a day. She had no weight loss, pain after eating, blood in her stool, or nighttime bowel movements. Over-the-counter loperamide helped modestly.
Her history was complex. She had previously been treated for cancer of the appendix with partial removal of the right colon, and she also had mixed connective tissue disease and high blood pressure.
Early tests were unrevealing. Screening for celiac disease and thyroid problems was normal; she was not anemic, and a recent CT scan of her abdomen and pelvis showed nothing abnormal. Doctors scheduled an endoscopy of both the upper and lower digestive tract.
The Pouch That Gave the Case Its Name
During the upper endoscopy, the team found an inverted pouch arising from the medial wall of the second part of the duodenum, just above the major papilla, the opening where bile and pancreatic juices enter the gut. The authors titled their report "Gone With the Windsock Diverticulum" and included a photo of an aviation windsock beside a hospital helipad to show the resemblance. Endoscopic images showed the pouch's dome and a notched, partly firm opening, with the true channel of the duodenum running alongside.
Most diverticula bulge outward from the bowel wall. This kind sits inside the channel food travels through. Its estimated prevalence is less than 0.05%. It is thought to arise around the seventh week of embryonic development, when a thin membrane in the duodenum fails to clear properly as the gut forms its hollow channel.
The location in this case is typical. A 2008 report on duodenal windsock webs noted that the second portion of the duodenum accounts for 85% to 90% of windsock cases. The anomaly has turned up at the same Arizona campus before, in a 2018 report of an incidental windsock diverticulum found in a 55-year-old man evaluated for trouble swallowing.
Innocent Bystander or Hidden Culprit
The pouch looked benign, with no inflamed, ulcerated, or suspicious tissue, so doctors did not biopsy it. They did take samples elsewhere. Biopsies of the duodenal lining showed no celiac disease, Whipple's disease, or Giardia infection, and fluid samples found no bacterial overgrowth in the small intestine. A colonoscopy was normal, and colon biopsies ruled out inflammatory and microscopic colitis.
That left the diverticulum as the only unusual finding, but the authors could not establish it as the cause of her diarrhea. In other published cases, these pouches have caused more dramatic problems, including partial blockage of the duodenum, bleeding and inflammation of the pancreas.
A report in the Turkish Journal of Gastroenterology, published online in 2025, described a 22-year-old woman whose windsock diverticulum caused repeated bouts of pancreatitis. Doctors removed it with an endoscopic snare, and she had no further episodes over nine months of follow-up.
The pouch tissue is rich in blood vessels, but no published cases suggest it can turn cancerous, according to the Mayo authors.
Removal Carries Risks of Its Own
Symptomatic windsock diverticula can be cut out or divided during endoscopy using a wire snare or specialized knives, and a series of five endoscopic treatments illustrated the range of techniques. These procedures can cause immediate or delayed bleeding that may require clips or cauterization. Patients with acute bowel obstruction may need laparoscopic surgery to remove part of the duodenum.
Because her symptoms were mild and no causal link was proven, the woman chose not to have the pouch removed. She is managing her diarrhea with loperamide and diet changes, and doctors will watch for signs of blockage after meals, pancreatitis, or bleeding. If her diarrhea persists or worsens with no other explanation, the diverticulum will be reconsidered as a cause.
The authors argue that simply recognizing the anomaly's characteristic look can spare patients unnecessary scans or endoscopic ultrasound. This is a single case, and it cannot show how often these pouches cause symptoms in older adults. The case was previously presented at the American College of Gastroenterology's 2025 annual meeting in Phoenix.
Anyone with ongoing changes in bowel habits should discuss them with a doctor, who can decide whether tests such as endoscopy are needed.
Key Questions Answered
What is a windsock diverticulum?
It is a rare pouch that projects into the inside of the duodenum, named for its resemblance to an airfield windsock.
How did doctors find it?
During a routine upper endoscopy for a 76-year-old woman's year-long chronic diarrhea.
Is the condition present from birth?
It is thought to be congenital, forming around the seventh week of embryonic development when a membrane in the duodenum fails to clear properly.
Did it cause her diarrhea?
Doctors could not prove it did. Other tests were negative, but no causal link was established.
What complications can it cause?
Published cases describe partial duodenal blockage, bleeding, and pancreatitis.
Does it need to be removed?
Not always. She chose monitoring because her symptoms were mild and removal can cause bleeding.
